summary.oneLiner: Yuken India Limited is a Bengaluru-based hydraulics and fluid-power manufacturer, affiliated to Japan's Yuken Kogyo Co Limited, making hydraulic pumps, valves and systems alongside an in-house cast-iron foundry business.
summary.business: Yuken India operates in the hydraulics / fluid power segment of the capital goods industry, catering to sectors such as steel, power, construction, machine tools, plastics and heavy engineering. The Group reports two business segments: a hydraulic business consisting of hydraulic pumps, valves and hydraulic systems, and a foundry business consisting of cast iron castings. India is the only major geographical segment, constituting over 95% of the Group's revenues, with a small export stream; no single customer contributes 10 percent or more of total revenue.

Hydraulic business: Customized hydraulic systems for defence, export, agriculture and mobile applications

currentContext.expansion: The annual report contains no named expansion project, no commissioning or ramp-up timeline and no capacity-addition narrative. The only expansion signal is indirect and retrospective: the Board's Report outlook states that FY26 profitability 'was impacted by higher operating costs, increased employee expenses and depreciation charges arising from investments in capacity and infrastructure', and the MD&A attributes the year's higher depreciation and amortisation to 'capital expenditure undertaken during the year'. Funding-side, the promoter Yuken Kogyo Company Limited, Japan subscribed to a preferential allotment of 5,84,000 equity shares at Rs 10 face value plus a premium of Rs 1,016 per share, described in the MD&A as a 'capital infusion by the Promoter amounting to H59.91 Crores, resulting in improvement in the capital base of the Company'; no use-of-proceeds or project is named against it. On the group side, AEPL Grotek Renewable Energy Private Limited - a step-down subsidiary in which Grotek Enterprises Private Limited holds 51% of voting power - appears to be in a build-up phase (its total income rose while it recorded a loss for the year), and the Board approved a fresh corporate guarantee of Rs 240 lakhs to it (Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation) at its meeting held on 13-08-2025; the report does not describe the underlying renewable-energy project, its size or its timeline. Forward-looking language in the MD&A outlook is generic - the industry is expected to see 'gradual but uneven industrial recovery' and 'increasing emphasis on energy efficiency, automation, and technologically advanced hydraulic solutions will require continuous investment in product development and innovation' - with no project, quantum or date attached.
currentContext.mdna: Management expects to operate 'in an environment of gradual but uneven industrial recovery, supported by sustained domestic capital expenditure and continued focus on manufacturing-led growth in India'|Outlook for the hydraulics and fluid power industry described as 'stable with moderate growth potential', driven by infrastructure development, expansion in core sectors such as steel, power, railways and defence, and increasing automation across manufacturing processes|'China+1' supply chain realignment expected to create additional opportunities for domestic players in engineering and precision components|Demand for standard hydraulic products and aftermarket services 'likely to remain steady, supported by a growing installed base and recurring maintenance requirements'|Systems and project-based segment 'expected to improve gradually, in line with revival in capital-intensive projects and improved execution cycles'|Government-led capital expenditure, infrastructure development and PLI schemes supporting domestic demand across engineering industries|Revenue mix is concentrated: Machine Tools at roughly 47% of FY26 sales is the dominant driver, so performance is 'sensitive to manufacturing investment cycles'; Steel, Plastics and Construction together at ~27% provide a stable baseline|Headwinds flagged: global uncertainties, input cost fluctuations and competitive pressures 'could impact margins and order visibility in the short term'|Industry-level margin pressure from rising input costs and competitive intensity, with both domestic players and global entrants expanding their presence|Structural shift in the sector towards automation, digitalisation, energy-efficient hydraulic systems, cost optimisation and localisation of supply chains|FY26 profitability was pressured by higher operating costs, increased employee expenses and depreciation charges arising from investments in capacity and infrastructure, against only marginal revenue growth|No order book or pipeline figure is disclosed in this bundle. Management refers only qualitatively to order flows: 'global trade disruptions and industrial slowdown in certain export markets led to volatility in order flows', and warns that global uncertainties, input cost fluctuations and competitive pressures 'could impact margins and order visibility in the short term'.

risks.risk: Cyclical demand tied to industrial and capital-expenditure cycles
risks.note: Management states the business 'is dependent on core sectors such as steel, construction, machine tools, and infrastructure, which are cyclical in nature' and that 'any slowdown in capital investment or industrial activity may impact demand for hydraulic products and systems'. Revenue is not just cyclical but concentrated within the cycle: Machine Tools alone is roughly 47% of FY26 sales, which the MD&A says makes performance 'sensitive to manufacturing investment cycles'.

risks.risk: Input cost volatility with imperfect pass-through
risks.note: The MD&A flags that 'fluctuations in prices of steel, castings, and other raw materials can impact cost structures and put pressure on margins if not fully passed on to customers'. The industry section adds that the sector faced margin pressure during FY26 from rising input costs, and FY26 profit before tax fell despite roughly flat revenue - so the pass-through gap is already visible, not hypothetical.

risks.risk: Technological substitution away from traditional hydraulics
risks.note: Management explicitly flags 'increasing adoption of alternative technologies such as electro-mechanical systems and advanced automation solutions', and lists 'Technological Substitution' among threats: a 'shift towards electro-mechanical and alternative motion control technologies may impact traditional hydraulics demand'. This is the one structural risk that could erode the addressable market rather than merely defer it, and the stated response - continuous investment in product development - is an ongoing cost.

risks.risk: Competitive intensity from domestic and global players
risks.note: The MD&A describes 'competition from both domestic and international players, leading to pricing pressures and the need for continuous product innovation and efficiency improvement', and notes in the industry section that 'both domestic players and global entrants' are expanding their presence in India. The China+1 opportunity that helps Yuken also attracts entrants to the same market.

risks.risk: Project execution risk on the systems / project-based portion of revenue
risks.note: Management notes 'a portion of revenues is derived from project-based systems, which are subject to delays in execution, extended approval cycles, and variability in customer spending timelines'. The outlook expects this segment to improve only 'gradually, in line with revival in capital-intensive projects and improved execution cycles', so timing risk sits on the part of the mix management is counting on for recovery.

risks.risk: Foreign-currency exposure on an import-weighted trade book
risks.note: The financial risk management note states the Group 'operates internationally and a significant portion of the business is transacted in USD, JPY, GBP and EURO', with exposure 'through its sales and purchases from overseas suppliers'. Foreign-currency trade payables (largely USD, including group sourcing from Yuken affiliates in Taiwan, China and Japan) exceed foreign-currency receivables, so the exposure is net-import - a depreciating rupee raises costs rather than helping. The note warns the exchange rate 'has changed substantially in recent years and may fluctuate substantially in the future'.

risks.risk: Interest-rate and liquidity exposure on largely floating-rate, short-dated borrowings
risks.note: Almost all Group borrowings carry variable interest rates, and the maturity profile shows the great majority of financial liabilities falling due within one year, with working-capital lines repayable on demand. Several of those limits are secured only by corporate guarantees from the Japanese parent Yuken Kogyo rather than by company assets, so continued access depends on the parent's willingness to keep renewing support alongside the mortgaged factory properties at Malur, Doddanekundi and Peenya.

risks.risk: Global trade fragmentation and geopolitical disruption
risks.note: Management flags 'ongoing geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions, and supply chain realignments' as creating uncertainty 'affecting export opportunities and input availability'. FY26 saw 'heightened trade fragmentation, driven by tariff measures and retaliatory actions', which the MD&A says produced 'volatility in order flows' from export markets - relevant both to the small but strategically prioritised export stream and to the Yuken group's cross-border sourcing.

risks.risk: Receivables concentration by ageing and slow collection
risks.note: Credit terms run 0 to 120 days and the expected-credit-loss table shows loss rates rising steeply with age - roughly 4% at 6-12 months and around 72% beyond three years - against a receivable book that is a large share of annual revenue. The offsetting comfort management gives is genuine breadth: 'no single customer contributes to more than 10 percent of outstanding trade receivables' and the base 'includes public sector enterprises and reputed private corporates'.

risks.risk: Regulatory and compliance change affecting product design and manufacturing
risks.note: Management flags that 'changes in industrial, environmental, or safety regulations may require continuous adaptation in product design and manufacturing processes'. This is stated as a live risk rather than as governance boilerplate, and sits alongside the energy-efficiency shift already reshaping product requirements.
